e-9535.problem: Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (3x+2) \: \mathbf{i} - y^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ and let $C$ be a path in $\mathbb R^2.$ Write $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}$ in the form $\displaystyle\int_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x +  Q(x,y)\,\textrm d y.$
e-9535.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y) \: \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y) \: \mathbf{j}
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y) \: \text{d}x + Q(x,y) \: \text{d}y.
$$

In our case, $P = 3x+2$ and $Q = -y^3.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6319.knowledge_point: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
e-6319.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/38ab4af726729b5c9804f4aa13801d637e5e62eda085d6611174586827ef8c11.png)

Consider the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $FGHF$ shown above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction. Express this integral as a sum of line integrals along $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3.$
e-6319.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3,
$$

where $-C_1$ and $-C_2$ are the same paths as $C_1$ and $C_2$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6286.knowledge_point: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
e-6286.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/001487e4a94988a24d15702a18692e9deb2495a7cc7ec5c9f71b98fea13e0ce8.png)

The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $O(0,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
e-6286.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let F(x,y,z)=y2i−x2j+5k and let C be a path in R3. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
 ∫Cy2dx−x2dy+5dz
b
 ∫C(y2−x2)dxdy+5dz
c
 ∫C(y2+x2+5)dxdydz
d
 ∫Cy2dx+x2dy
e
∫Cx2dx−y2dy+5dz
Submit

decision.explanation: Since dr = i dx + j dy + k dz, the dot product is F·dr = y² dx − x² dy + 5 dz. Integrating along C gives option a.

Question 1
?

Let F(x,y,z)=y2i−x2j+5k and let C be a path in R3. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
 ∫Cy2dx−x2dy+5dz
b
 ∫C(y2−x2)dxdy+5dz
c
 ∫C(y2+x2+5)dxdydz
d
 ∫Cy2dx+x2dy
e
∫Cx2dx−y2dy+5dz
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field

F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)i+Q(x,y,z)j+R(x,y,z)k defined on C, we have

∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y,z)dx+Q(x,y,z)dy+R(x,y,z)dz.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫Cy2dx−x2dy+5dz.

verification.explanation: The dot product F·dr equals y² dx − x² dy + 5 dz, so option a is correct. The revealed worked solution confirms this; the incorrect feedback applies to the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
content.problem: Let $F(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\,i-{x}^{2}\,j+5\,k$ and let $C$ be a path in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
content.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y+5\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Let F(x,y)=4i−(2y−3x)j and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t,3t−1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫C(3x−1)dx+ydy
b
∫Cxdx+(3y−1)dy
c
∫C4dx−(2y−3x)dy
d
 ∫C(2y−3x)dx−4dy
e
∫C(3y−1)dx+xdy
Submit

decision.explanation: For F = P i + Q j, F·dr = P dx + Q dy. Here P = 4 and Q = −(2y−3x), giving option c directly.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Let $F(x,y)=4\,i-(2y-3x)\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨t,\,3t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
after.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}4\,\text{d}x-(2y-3x)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Let F(x,y)=4i−(2y−3x)j and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t,3t−1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫C(3x−1)dx+ydy
b
∫Cxdx+(3y−1)dy
c
∫C4dx−(2y−3x)dy
d
 ∫C(2y−3x)dx−4dy
e
∫C(3y−1)dx+xdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)j

defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C4dx−(2y−3x)dy.

content.problem: Let $F(x,y)=4\,i-(2y-3x)\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨t,\,3t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
content.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}4\,\text{d}x-(2y-3x)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: If ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+y\,\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z$ is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $F(x,y,z)=$
after.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+R\,\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P={x}^{2},Q=y,R={z}^{3}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}\,i+y\,j+{z}^{3}\,k)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+y\,\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)i+Q(x,y,z)j+R(x,y,z)k defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CPdx+Qdy+Rdz

content.problem: If ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+y\,\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z$ is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $F(x,y,z)=$
content.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+R\,\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P={x}^{2},Q=y,R={z}^{3}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}\,i+y\,j+{z}^{3}\,k)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+y\,\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $F={x}^{2}\,i+y\,j+{z}^{3}\,k.$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Let F(x,y)=(x−3y)i+2j and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t,t2+1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫C2dx+(x−3y)dy
b
∫C(x2+1)dx+ydy
c
∫C(y2+1)dx+xdy
d
∫C(x−3y)dx+2dy
e
∫Cxdx+(y2+1)dy
Submit

decision.explanation: Since dr = i dx + j dy, F·dr = (x−3y) dx + 2 dy. Therefore the equivalent line integral is option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Let $F(x,y)=(x-3y)\,i+2\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2}+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
after.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(x-3y)\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Let F(x,y)=(x−3y)i+2j and let C be the path defined by r(t)=⟨t,t2+1⟩ for t∈[0,1]. Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr?

a
∫C2dx+(x−3y)dy
b
∫C(x2+1)dx+ydy
c
∫C(y2+1)dx+xdy
d
∫C(x−3y)dx+2dy
e
∫Cxdx+(y2+1)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)j

defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CP(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy.

Therefore, in our case, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C(x−3y)dx+2dy.

content.problem: Let $F(x,y)=(x-3y)\,i+2\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2}+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
content.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(x-3y)\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: If ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-y\,\text{d}y+2z\,\text{d}z$ is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $F(x,y,z)=$
after.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+R\,\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P={x}^{2},Q=-y,R=2z.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}\,i-y\,j+2z\,k)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-y\,\text{d}y+2z\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Submit

EXPLANATION

Given a piecewise-smooth path C and a vector field F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)i+Q(x,y,z)j+R(x,y,z)k defined on C, we have ∫CF⋅dr=∫CPdx+Qdy+Rdz

In our case, P=x2,Q=−y,R=2z. Therefore

∫C(x2i−yj+2zk)⋅dr=∫Cx2dx−ydy+2zdz.

So, F=x2i−yj+2zk.

content.problem: If ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-y\,\text{d}y+2z\,\text{d}z$ is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $F(x,y,z)=$
content.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+R\,\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P={x}^{2},Q=-y,R=2z.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}\,i-y\,j+2z\,k)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-y\,\text{d}y+2z\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $F={x}^{2}\,i-y\,j+2z\,k.$

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path LMNL, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit

decision.explanation: The counterclockwise path L→M→N→L follows C₁, reverses C₂ (shown N→M), and follows C₃ (shown N→L). Reversing a path negates its line integral, so the sum is ∫C₁ F·dr − ∫C₂ F·dr + ∫C₃ F·dr, option b.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/fec5c3e96eeed9fb01479c0127e2d530a628855a124d8ab1ef380c48c2f569f1.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $LMNL,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path LMNL, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C2 is the same path as C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/fec5c3e96eeed9fb01479c0127e2d530a628855a124d8ab1ef380c48c2f569f1.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $LMNL,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path KMLK, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit

decision.explanation: The clockwise path K→M→L→K follows C₁, reverses C₂ (L→M), and reverses C₃ (K→L). Reversing a path negates its line integral, giving option a.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/5484647a9c694b95bd9e4b569c84f7263c5e69de5e98f12a1081fd937d298769.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $KMLK,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {-{C}_{3}},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path KMLK, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed clockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪{−C3},

where −C2 and −C3 are the same paths as C2 and C3 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫−C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr.

verification.explanation: The path K→M→L→K follows C₁ and reverses both C₂ and C₃. Reversal negates a line integral, yielding option a, as confirmed by the worked solution. The incorrect feedback applies to the deliberately submitted option c.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/5484647a9c694b95bd9e4b569c84f7263c5e69de5e98f12a1081fd937d298769.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $KMLK,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {-{C}_{3}},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path OGHO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit

decision.explanation: The counterclockwise path O→G→H→O reverses C₁ (G→O), reverses C₂ (H→G), and follows C₃ (H→O). Reversing a path negates its integral, so option b is correct.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/801321d1639e668c3778c198df9a5b98ea3e6018f12ab2e5c756bfa4f04cb574.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OGHO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={-{C}_{1}}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ and $-{C}_{2}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path OGHO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C={−C1}∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C1 and −C2 are the same paths as C1 and C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫−C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/801321d1639e668c3778c198df9a5b98ea3e6018f12ab2e5c756bfa4f04cb574.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OGHO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={-{C}_{1}}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ and $-{C}_{2}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$
history.html:
First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C={−C1}∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C1 and −C2 are the same paths as C1 and C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫−C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path ODEO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit

decision.explanation: The counterclockwise path O→D→E→O follows C₁ (O→D), reverses C₂ (E→D), and reverses C₃ (O→E). Reversing a path negates its integral, giving option e.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/a42c95d0604d9855fb00ac9b7f2a1d2f9db0dd9c6beb3b68750a074818c99dc8.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $ODEO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths: 

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {-{C}_{3}},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path ODEO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
c
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪{−C3},

where −C2 and −C3 are the same paths as C2 and C3 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫−C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr.

verification.explanation: O→D follows C₁, D→E reverses C₂, and E→O reverses C₃. Reversing a path negates its line integral, giving option e, consistent with the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option c.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/a42c95d0604d9855fb00ac9b7f2a1d2f9db0dd9c6beb3b68750a074818c99dc8.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $ODEO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths: 

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {-{C}_{3}},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path OABO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit

decision.explanation: The counterclockwise path O→A→B→O follows C₁ (O→A), reverses C₂ (B→A), and follows C₃ (B→O). Reversing a path negates its integral, giving option a.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/103c586778cdd8181fdc8396a92472df0525fc8e1c77fde9a7c3f731dca6df07.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OABO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where C is the closed polygonal path OABO, shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?

a
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
b
∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr
c
∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
d
−∫C1F⋅dr+∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
e
−∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr−∫C3F⋅dr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can represent C, which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of 3 paths:

C=C1∪{−C2}∪C3,

where −C2 is the same path as C2 but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

∫CF⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr+∫−C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr=∫C1F⋅dr−∫C2F⋅dr+∫C3F⋅dr.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/103c586778cdd8181fdc8396a92472df0525fc8e1c77fde9a7c3f731dca6df07.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OABO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2-t,t⟩ \\  & =(2-t)\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=2-t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j \\  & =(2-t+t)\,i+(2-t-t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(2-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i+(2-2t)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =-2+(2-2t) \\  & =-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-(1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/73c6a8268a179f72611fb65e099d1249d48501e4fd4731d03747800e1944fd97.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,2)$ to the point $D(1,3).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+t(⟨1,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\  & =⟨t,1+t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j \\  & =(2t-3(1+t))\,i+(t+(1+t))\,j \\  & =(-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =((-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-3-t+2t+1 \\  & =t-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-2t]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-2-0]+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $B$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(0-b) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+t(⟨0,0⟩-⟨1,1⟩) \\  & =⟨1-t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(1-t)\,i+(1-t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=1-t$ and $y=1-t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2(1-t)+(1-t))\,i+((1-t)-2(1-t))\,j \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j)\cdot (-i-j) \\  & =-3+3t+1-t \\  & =-2+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+(-2t+{t}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+(1-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,-1)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,1)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $B$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(0-b) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+t(⟨0,0⟩-⟨1,1⟩) \\  & =⟨1-t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(1-t)\,i+(1-t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=1-t$ and $y=1-t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2(1-t)+(1-t))\,i+((1-t)-2(1-t))\,j \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j)\cdot (-i-j) \\  & =-3+3t+1-t \\  & =-2+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+(-2t+{t}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+(1-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
